reason: The hypothesis relies on the premise that APT-derived microstructural features can be used as ML inputs to predict mechanical properties, but none of the cited evidence demonstrates APT-based feature extraction, links APT data to mechanical response, or validates the claimed accuracy and speed gains for HfNbTiVAl10. E1 discusses DFT limitations and physics-based models, E2 notes general ML use for HEA properties with composition/physics-based features, and E3 describes genetic algorithm feature selection without mentioning APT. The key premises are therefore unsupported by the cited passages.
premises: APT can extract microstructural descriptors (grain boundary chemistry, precipitate size/distribution, local ordering) that quantify bonding environments and interfacial characteristics relevant to mec
These APT-derived descriptors can serve as input features for a machine-learning model to predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior.
A physics-informed ML model (e.g., gradient boosting regression) trained on such descriptors can achieve 20–30% lower prediction errors than conventional simulations.
The ML approach reduces prediction time by orders of magnitude compared to DFT/molecular dynamics simulations.
The method remains valid as long as the hierarchical structure is stable relative to the APT sampling period and the tested microstructure falls within the training distribution.
